name: Saving web pages as PDF
title: How to save any web page as a PDF, on any device
metaTitle: How to Save a Web Page as PDF (2026 Guide)
metaDescription: Save any web page as a PDF in Chrome, Safari, Firefox, Edge, iPhone or Android. Print-to-PDF, full-page screenshots, and archiving that survives link rot.
intro: Every browser can turn a web page into a PDF, and every browser hides the option somewhere slightly different. These guides cover the desktop print dialog, the iPhone Share sheet, full-page screenshot capture when the layout matters more than the text, and proper archiving for pages you need to still exist in five years. Along the way: which methods keep links clickable, which produce a searchable file, and which quietly hand you a picture of text.
answer: Press Ctrl+P (Cmd+P on Mac), change the destination to "Save as PDF" and click Save. On iPhone, use the Share sheet, tap Options and choose PDF. Both keep the text selectable and the links clickable, unlike a screenshot, which stores pixels only.
primaryKeyword: how to save a web page as a pdf

posts.title: How to save a web page as a PDF in any browser
posts.metaTitle: Save a Web Page as PDF in Any Browser
posts.metaDescription: Save a web page as a PDF in Chrome, Safari, Firefox and Edge. The shortcut, Microsoft Print to PDF, page ranges, and how to keep the links clickable.
posts.primaryKeyword: how to save a web page as a pdf
posts.answer: Press Ctrl+P on Windows or Cmd+P on a Mac, open the Destination list and choose Save as PDF, then click Save. Every desktop browser supports this. The resulting file keeps selectable text and clickable links, and you can limit it to a page range before saving.

body.x: There is no "Save as PDF" item in any browser File menu, which is why this question gets asked so often. The feature lives inside the print dialog, disguised as a printer. You never send anything to a printer; the browser renders the page to a file instead.
The shortcut that works in every desktop browser

items.h: Scroll to the bottom of the page first
items.x: Modern sites lazy-load images, meaning a photo is only fetched once you scroll near it. Anything you never scrolled past will be a blank box in the PDF. One quick End key press fixes it.
Use the keyboard, not the right-click menu. On a few sites the right-click Print item is intercepted by the page and prints the wrong frame.
At the top of the dialog, open **Destination** (Chrome, Edge) or **Printer** (Firefox) and pick **Save as PDF** or **Save to PDF**.
Look at the preview. If your content is on sheets 2 to 4 of a nine-sheet monster, type `2-4` in the Pages box rather than saving all nine.
Turn **Headers and footers** off to drop the browser-added title, URL, date and page number. Leave **Background graphics** off unless you specifically want the coloured blocks.
Choose a folder and a filename. The file is written locally; nothing is uploaded anywhere.

body.caption: Where the PDF option hides, by browser.
head: Browser
Menu label
Extras worth knowing
rows: Keeps links clickable and text selectable. "Print using system dialog" gives you the OS printer sheet instead.
Also offers Microsoft Print to PDF as a separate, worse option. Pick the Edge one.
Firefox remembers the choice for the rest of the session.
PDF ▾ button, bottom-left of the print sheet → Save as PDF
Also has File → Export as PDF, which produces one continuous unpaginated page.
Identical to Chrome; they share the same print engine.

body.x: Windows: Save as PDF is not the same as Microsoft Print to PDF
Windows 10 and 11 ship a virtual printer called **Microsoft Print to PDF**, and it shows up in the same dropdown as the browser’s own option. They are not interchangeable.

head: Chrome/Edge "Save as PDF"
Microsoft Print to PDF
rows: Yes, any Windows app with a Print command

body.x: Use Microsoft Print to PDF when you need a PDF from an app that has no PDF export of its own. For web pages, the browser option is better on every measure that matters.
Safari has two routes and they produce different files

**Cmd+P → PDF ▾ → Save as PDF** paginates the page into Letter or A4 sheets, exactly like printing. **File → Export as PDF** produces a single page as tall as the whole document, with no page breaks at all. The second is excellent for keeping a layout intact and terrible for printing later, because most printers will shrink that one enormous page to fit a single sheet.

Before you save, use Safari Reader (⌃⌘R) or Firefox Reader View (F9). The PDF then contains the article and nothing else, typically two pages instead of nine. See [printing a web page without ads](/blog/print/print-web-page-without-ads) for the full set of cleanup methods.
Save the page you want, not the page the site hands you

A PDF made from a raw web page inherits every problem the printed version would have: ad slots, a cookie banner frozen mid-page, a "related stories" grid, and a newsletter box. The fix is to clean first and save second.

items: Paste the URL into the [web page printer](/print).
Click any block you do not want to remove it. Drag to sweep several at once, Ctrl+Z to undo.
Set text size and image size in the Style menu.
Press **Download PDF**, or **Print** and choose Save as PDF for a smaller, fully searchable file.

body.x: Already have a saved .html file or some HTML you wrote yourself? Convert it straight to PDF in the browser.
Phones and tablets

On iPhone and iPad the route is the Share sheet, not a print dialog: see [saving a web page as a PDF on iPhone](/blog/save-pdf/save-webpage-as-pdf-iphone). On Android, Chrome uses the same print flow as the desktop: tap **⋮ → Share → Print**, then choose **Save as PDF** as the printer. The file lands in your Downloads folder and appears in the Files app.
When a PDF is the wrong output

items: You need the **visual layout preserved exactly**, including a sticky header or an interactive chart. Take a [full-page screenshot](/blog/save-pdf/full-page-screenshot) instead.
You need **third-party proof of what the page said**. A self-made PDF proves nothing on its own. [Archive the page properly](/blog/save-pdf/archive-web-pages).
You need to **edit the text afterwards**. Copy it into a document, or convert the PDF to Word later.
The page is behind a **login you cannot keep**. Print-to-PDF works while you are signed in, so save it before the session expires.

body.x: A PDF saved from a page carries the page metadata plus your own: author name from your OS user account, creation timestamp, and sometimes the local file path. Strip it before sending anything sensitive, using [remove metadata](/tools/remove-metadata).
Keeping the file small

A text-heavy article saves at 100 to 300 KB. A photo essay or a product page full of hero images can reach 15 MB, which is enough to bounce off an email attachment limit. Two levers: turn images off in a cleaner before saving, or run the finished PDF through compression. A 15 MB image-heavy page usually lands between 1 and 3 MB after compression with no visible loss on screen.
Saved a PDF that turned out to be 20 MB? Compress it without uploading it anywhere.

faqs.q: Why is "Save as PDF" missing from my print dialog?
faqs.a: You are probably looking at the operating system print sheet rather than the browser one. In Chrome, click "Print using system dialog" to switch between them; the browser dialog is the one with the Destination dropdown. On Windows, check that the Microsoft Print to PDF feature has not been turned off in Windows Features.

faqs.q: Does saving a web page as a PDF keep the links working?
faqs.a: Yes, when you use the browser built-in Save as PDF in Chrome, Edge, Firefox or Safari. Links become clickable annotations in the file. Microsoft Print to PDF and image-based exports both lose them.

faqs.q: How do I save a web page as a PDF without the ads?
faqs.a: Turn on Reader mode before pressing Ctrl+P, or paste the URL into a printer-friendly tool and delete the remaining blocks by hand. Either approach usually cuts a nine-page save to two or three pages.

faqs.q: Can I save a whole website as a PDF, not just one page?
faqs.a: Not in one click. The print dialog handles the current page only. For a multi-page save, save each page separately and then merge the PDFs into a single document, which also lets you set the chapter order.

faqs.q: Is the saved PDF searchable?
faqs.a: Yes. Print-to-PDF writes real text, so Ctrl+F works inside the file and search indexes on your computer can read it. A screenshot saved as a PDF is an image and needs OCR before it becomes searchable.

posts.title: How to save a web page as a PDF on iPhone and iPad
posts.metaTitle: Save a Web Page as PDF on iPhone or iPad
posts.metaDescription: Three ways to save a web page as a PDF on iPhone and iPad: the Share sheet Options menu, a Full Page screenshot, and Print preview. Save to Files or Books.
posts.primaryKeyword: save web page as pdf iphone
posts.answer: On iPhone and iPad, open the page in Safari, tap the Share button, tap Options under the page title, choose PDF, then tap Save to Files. For a picture-perfect copy instead, take a screenshot, tap the thumbnail, switch to Full Page and save the PDF.

body.x: iOS gives you three different PDFs from the same web page, and they are genuinely different files. One is the article text reflowed for reading, one is the page exactly as it renders, and one is a paginated print job. Picking the wrong one is why people end up with a PDF full of ads or a PDF missing half the page.
Method 1: Share sheet → Options → PDF (best for text)

items.x: This route is Safari-only. Chrome and Firefox on iOS do not expose it.
The square with an upward arrow, at the bottom of the screen on iPhone and in the toolbar on iPad.

It sits directly under the page title and site name at the top of the Share sheet, showing the current setting, usually **Automatic**. It is easy to miss because it looks like a label rather than a button.
Four choices appear: Automatic, Reader PDF, PDF and Web Archive. **PDF** captures the page as rendered. **Reader PDF** captures the stripped-down article and is the one you usually want.

items.h: Tap Done, then Save to Files
items.x: Pick iCloud Drive or On My iPhone, rename the file, and tap Save.

body.x: **Reader PDF** is only offered when Safari can see an article on the page. If the option is greyed out, the page is a dashboard, a form or a JavaScript app, and only the plain PDF option is available.
Method 2: Full Page screenshot (best for layout)

This is the most reliable option and almost nobody knows it exists. It captures the entire scrolling page, not just what is on screen, and hands you a real PDF. The desktop equivalents are covered in [taking a full-page screenshot](/blog/save-pdf/full-page-screenshot).

items.x: Press **Side button + Volume Up** on Face ID devices, or **Home + Side button** on Touch ID devices.
It appears in the bottom-left corner for about five seconds. Tap it before it disappears.
Two tabs sit at the top of the editor: **Screen** and **Full Page**. Tap **Full Page**. A scrollable strip on the right shows the whole document.
Drag the handles on the right-hand strip to trim the top and bottom. Use the pen, highlighter and text tools to annotate before saving.
Tap **Done → Save PDF to Files**. Full Page captures can only be saved as PDF, never to Photos, which is why the option reads the way it does.

body.x: Full Page works in Safari, Mail, Notes, Files, Pages and Maps. It does not work in most third-party apps, which fall back to the visible screen only.
Method 3: Print preview pinch (the old trick)

Before iOS 13 added the Options menu, everyone used this: Share → **Print**, then pinch outwards on the page preview thumbnail. The preview expands into a full PDF viewer, and the Share button in the corner lets you save it. It still works, and it is the only way to get a **paginated** PDF on iOS, with real Letter or A4 page breaks, which matters if someone will print the file later.

body.caption: Which iOS method to use.
head: You want…
Method
Result
rows: Text only, links kept, small file, no ads
The page exactly as it looks
Pixel-accurate, one tall page, no selectable text
Something you will print on paper
Proper page breaks at Letter or A4
A copy that works offline forever
.webarchive file, Safari only, keeps images and CSS
Handwriting, highlights and text boxes baked in

body.x: Where the file actually goes

**Save to Files** offers iCloud Drive, which syncs to your Mac where [the desktop print dialog](/blog/save-pdf/save-webpage-as-pdf-chrome) gives you more control, and On My iPhone (stays on the device, survives no backup unless you back the device up). If you tap the **Books** icon in the Share sheet instead, the PDF is imported into Apple Books, where it gets a reading position, bookmarks and highlights, and syncs across your devices. Books is the better home for long documents you will read; Files is the better home for receipts and records.
Saving to Books makes the file harder to email later. You have to open it in Books, tap Share, then Save to Files. If you might need to send it, save to Files first and add it to Books afterwards.
Chrome, Firefox and Edge on iOS

Every iOS browser uses Apple’s WebKit engine, but only Safari gets the Options → PDF menu. In Chrome for iOS, tap **⋯ → Print**, then use the same pinch-out trick. Firefox and Edge behave the same way. The Full Page screenshot method is Safari-only, so for anything important it is worth opening the link in Safari first.
Saved five pages of a long article separately? Merge them into one document in your browser.
Cleaning the page before you save

The mobile equivalent of a printer-friendly view is Safari Reader: tap the **☰ page menu** at the left of the address bar and choose **Show Reader**. Save from inside Reader and the PDF contains the article, headings and photos, with no navigation and no ad slots. If Reader is unavailable, the [web page printer](/print) works in mobile Safari too, and lets you delete blocks by tapping them. If the result is still heavy, run it through [compress PDF](/tools/compress-pdf) before emailing it.

faqs.q: Why can I not find Options in the Share sheet?
faqs.a: Options only appears in Safari, and only for web pages. It sits directly under the page title at the very top of the sheet, above the row of app icons, and reads "Options >" with the current mode next to it. If you are sharing from another app, it will not be there.

faqs.q: How do I save a web page as a PDF on iPad?
faqs.a: Exactly as on iPhone. The Share button is in the top toolbar instead of the bottom bar, and the Full Page screenshot thumbnail appears in the bottom-left after pressing the top button and Volume Up together, or Command+Shift+3 with a keyboard attached.

faqs.q: Can I save a web page as a PDF without Safari?
faqs.a: Yes, using Share → Print and pinching out on the preview, which works in Chrome, Firefox and Edge for iOS. You lose the Reader PDF and Full Page options, both of which are Safari features.

faqs.q: Does the iPhone PDF keep the links clickable?
faqs.a: The Share sheet PDF and Reader PDF keep links as clickable annotations. The Full Page screenshot does not, because it is an image wrapped in a PDF container.

faqs.q: How do I make the saved PDF smaller?
faqs.a: Use Reader PDF rather than the plain PDF, which drops the heavy hero images and ad creatives. If it is still large, run the file through a compressor before emailing it.

posts.title: How to take a full-page screenshot of a website
posts.metaTitle: How to Take a Full-Page Screenshot
posts.metaDescription: Capture an entire scrolling web page as one image. Chrome DevTools, Firefox and Edge built-in capture, Safari Web Inspector, and when a PDF beats a PNG.
posts.answer: In Chrome, open DevTools with F12, press Ctrl+Shift+P, type screenshot and choose Capture full size screenshot. Firefox and Edge have it built in: right-click the page and pick Take Screenshot, then Save full page. The result is one tall PNG of the entire scrolling page.

body.x: The screenshot key on your keyboard captures the screen, which is the wrong unit. A web page is usually four to ten screens tall. Every major browser can capture the whole thing in one image, but only Firefox and Edge put the feature somewhere you would find by accident.
Chrome: the DevTools command menu

items.h: Scroll to the bottom of the page
items.x: Lazy-loaded images below the fold have not been fetched yet and will capture as blank space. Press End, wait a second, then press Home.
Press **F12**, or **Ctrl+Shift+I** on Windows, or **Cmd+Option+I** on macOS.
Press **Ctrl+Shift+P** (**Cmd+Shift+P** on macOS). A search box appears at the top of DevTools.
Four options appear. Choose **Capture full size screenshot**. The others capture the visible area, a selected element, or a region you drag.
Chrome writes a PNG straight to your Downloads folder, named after the page. There is no save dialog.

body.x: Before capturing, use Ctrl+Shift+M in DevTools to switch to device mode and set an explicit width such as 1280 or 1440. The capture then has a predictable width instead of following your window size, which matters if you are producing several screenshots for the same document.
Firefox: right-click, no DevTools needed

Firefox has the best implementation of the three. Right-click anywhere on the page that is not a link or an image, choose **Take Screenshot**, then click **Save full page** in the top-right. A preview appears with Copy and Download buttons. You can also hover any element to capture just that block, which Firefox highlights with a dotted outline.
Microsoft Edge: Web capture

Press **Ctrl+Shift+S**, or use **⋯ → Screenshot**. Choose **Capture full page**. Edge then opens the capture in its own markup view where you can draw on it, copy it, or save it. Edge writes to Downloads as a JPEG by default rather than a PNG, which is worth knowing if you care about text sharpness.
Safari: Web Inspector

Safari needs the developer menu turned on: **Safari → Settings → Advanced → Show features for web developers**. Then press **Cmd+Option+I**, open the **Elements** tab, right-click the `<html>` node at the very top of the tree and choose **Capture Screenshot**. That captures the entire document. Right-clicking any other node captures just that element, which is a fast way to grab a single card or table.

body.caption: Full-page capture by browser, 2026.
head: Browser
How
Format
Notes
rows: No save dialog, goes straight to Downloads
Right-click → Take Screenshot → Save full page
Also captures a single hovered element
Opens a markup editor before saving
Web Inspector → Elements → right-click <html> → Capture Screenshot
Screenshot → tap thumbnail → Full Page tab
Cannot be saved as an image, only as PDF

body.x: What goes wrong on tall pages

items: **Sticky headers repeat.** A navigation bar with `position: fixed` is painted at each viewport position in some capture implementations, so it appears five times down the image. Delete the element in DevTools first, or scroll the page so the header un-sticks.
**Blank rectangles.** Lazy-loaded images that never entered the viewport. Always scroll to the bottom before capturing.

**Truncation on very long pages.** Browsers cap the capture at a maximum texture height, historically 16,384 pixels. An infinite-scroll feed will be cut off. Capture in two passes, or use the [print-to-PDF route](/blog/save-pdf/save-webpage-as-pdf-chrome) instead.
**Animations frozen mid-frame.** Carousels and skeleton loaders capture in whatever state they happen to be in.
**Cookie banners and chat bubbles.** They are part of the page. Dismiss them, or remove the node in DevTools before capturing.

body.x: PNG or PDF? They are not interchangeable

body.caption: The same 2,000-word article, captured two ways.
head: Full-page PNG
Print-to-PDF
rows: No, it reflows to paper width
Poorly, one huge image scaled to a sheet
Bug reports, design reviews, visual proof

body.x: If you need both properties, capture the PNG and also [save the page as a PDF](/blog/save-pdf/save-webpage-as-pdf-chrome). Together they cost under 10 MB and cover every later use.
Turn your PNG or JPG captures into PDF pages, then combine them into one document.
Making a screenshot searchable

A screenshot is an image, so nothing inside it can be found by search. Running it through [OCR](/tools/ocr-pdf) adds an invisible text layer underneath the pixels: the image looks identical, but Ctrl+F now works and the text can be copied. This is worth doing for anything you file away, because a folder of screenshots you cannot search is a folder you will never use again.
Add a searchable text layer to screenshots and scans without changing how they look.
Screenshots as evidence

A screenshot shows what you saw; it does not show when you saw it, and it is trivially editable. For a listing price, a policy change or a deleted post, pair the image with an independent capture from a third-party archive so the date does not depend on your word. That is covered in [archiving a web page](/blog/save-pdf/archive-web-pages).

faqs.q: How do I take a scrolling screenshot in Chrome without an extension?
faqs.a: Open DevTools with F12, press Ctrl+Shift+P, type "screenshot" and select Capture full size screenshot. Chrome saves a PNG of the entire page to your Downloads folder. No extension is needed and this has been built in since Chrome 59.

faqs.q: Why is my full-page screenshot cut off at the bottom?
faqs.a: Either the page loads more content as you scroll, so the browser measured the document before the rest arrived, or the page exceeds the maximum capture height of roughly 16,384 pixels. Scroll to the very bottom first, then capture; if it is still truncated, save as a PDF instead.

faqs.q: Why does the navigation bar appear several times in my screenshot?
faqs.a: It uses fixed positioning, so it is painted at every scroll offset the capture stitches together. Open DevTools, select the header element, press Delete, then take the screenshot.

faqs.q: Can I take a full-page screenshot on a phone?
faqs.a: On iPhone, take a screenshot, tap the thumbnail and switch to the Full Page tab, then save as PDF. On Android, take a screenshot and tap "Capture more" or "Scroll", though the exact label depends on the manufacturer.

faqs.q: Is a screenshot or a PDF better for saving a receipt?
faqs.a: A PDF. It is roughly twenty times smaller, the order number is searchable, and it prints properly. Take a screenshot as well only if the visual layout itself is what you need to prove.

posts.title: How to archive a web page so it still exists later
posts.metaTitle: How to Archive a Web Page That May Vanish
posts.metaDescription: Web pages disappear. Archive one properly with the Wayback Machine, a WARC capture, a PDF/A file or a dated screenshot, and know which method proves what.
posts.primaryKeyword: how to archive a web page
posts.answer: Archive a web page three ways at once: submit it to the Wayback Machine for a public, third-party-dated copy; save your own PDF for a readable offline record; and keep a full-page screenshot as visual proof. Public archives fail on paywalled or logged-in pages, so the local copy matters.

body.x: A bookmark is a promise that someone else will keep a page online for you. They frequently do not. Pew Research Center measured this in 2024 and found that **38 percent of web pages that existed in 2013 were no longer accessible ten years later**. Nearly a quarter of news pages they sampled already contained at least one dead link. If a page matters to you, the only reliable copy is one that does not depend on the publisher.
Three layers, because each one fails differently

body.caption: What each archiving method actually gives you.
head: Method
Proves the date
Survives your hard drive dying
Works behind a login
Keeps the text searchable

body.x: Layer 1: push it into a public archive

The Internet Archive has been crawling the web since 1996 and the Wayback Machine now holds well over 900 billion captures. You do not have to wait for a crawler to find your page. Go to **web.archive.org**, use the **Save Page Now** box, paste the URL and submit. The capture is timestamped by a third party, which is what makes it useful as evidence rather than merely as a backup.

items: **archive.today** (also reachable as archive.ph) stores both a rendered screenshot and the text, and often succeeds on pages the Wayback Machine cannot render.
**Perma.cc**, run by the Harvard Library Innovation Lab, is built for legal and academic citation and produces a permanent link that courts and journals accept.
None of the three can reach anything behind a login, a paywall or a country block. They see what an anonymous visitor sees.

body.x: Public archives honour removal requests and robots directives. A page you archived can later be withdrawn from the archive by the site owner. Never treat a public archive as your only copy of something that matters.
Layer 2: keep your own readable copy
This is the layer you control. The goal is a file that opens in twenty years without needing a specific browser version.

items.x: Paste the URL into the [web page printer](/print) and delete the banners, ad slots and comment sections. What remains is what you are actually archiving.

items.h: Save as PDF, not as an image
items.x: Use the browser Save as PDF destination so the text stays selectable. See [saving a page as a PDF](/blog/save-pdf/save-webpage-as-pdf-chrome).

items.h: Add the URL and date to the file itself
items.x: Browsers put both in the header and footer of a printout. For an archive copy, leave headers and footers ON: the provenance is more valuable than the tidier margin.

items.h: Name it so you can find it
items.x: A convention like `2026-04-09_example-com_pricing-page.pdf` sorts chronologically and survives being moved between folders.

items.h: Store two copies in two places
items.x: One local, one in cloud storage. A single copy in one location is not an archive.

body.x: Have the raw HTML saved already? Convert it to a PDF that opens anywhere.
PDF/A: the archival flavour of PDF

PDF/A is a restricted subset of PDF, standardised as **ISO 19005**, designed so a file renders identically decades from now. It embeds every font, forbids external references, JavaScript and encryption, and requires colour to be defined in device-independent terms. An ordinary PDF that links to a web font or relies on a viewer default can drift; a PDF/A cannot. For anything legal, medical or institutional, it is the right container. For a saved recipe, ordinary PDF is fine.
WARC: what real archivists use

A **WARC** file (Web ARChive, standardised as ISO 28500) stores the raw HTTP requests and responses for a page and everything it loads: HTML, CSS, JavaScript, images, fonts. Replaying a WARC reconstructs the page as a browser saw it, including interactive behaviour that a PDF flattens away. It is what the Internet Archive itself writes.

# One page plus its assets into a WARC, using wget
wget --warc-file=example --page-requisites --span-hosts \
     --convert-links --no-warc-compression \
     https://example.com/article

# Self-hosted archiving that writes WARC, PDF, screenshot and
# plain text for every URL you add
pip install archivebox && archivebox add "https://example.com/article"
A WARC is only useful with a replay tool. If nobody in your organisation knows how to open one, a PDF plus a screenshot is a more honest archive than a file format nobody can read.
When you need dated evidence, not just a copy
A PDF you made yourself proves what you saw. It does not prove when, because file timestamps are editable in seconds. If a dispute is plausible, add independent corroboration:

items: Submit the URL to the Wayback Machine and record the resulting capture link, which carries their timestamp, not yours.
Compute a checksum of your local file, for example `shasum -a 256 evidence.pdf`, and record it somewhere append-only such as a dated email to yourself.
For higher stakes, use an RFC 3161 trusted timestamp service, which signs the hash of your file with a time from an accredited authority.
Keep the original file untouched. Work on copies. A modified file breaks its own hash.

body.x: The quick version

items: **Casual bookmark you want to keep**, save a PDF and stop there.
**Research or references**, PDF plus a Wayback capture, filed with the date in the name.
**A price, offer or policy you may need to point at**, Wayback capture, PDF, and a full-page screenshot.
**Legal, academic or regulatory**, Perma.cc or a WARC, plus PDF/A, plus a hash.
**Something behind a login**, only your own copies work. Public archives cannot see it.

body.x: Combine a batch of archived pages into one dated dossier.

One last thing: strip the metadata before you share an archive with anyone else. A saved PDF carries your operating system username and often the local folder path, which is more than you meant to disclose. [Remove metadata](/blog/privacy/remove-metadata-from-pdf) covers what is in there.

faqs.q: How do I save a web page to the Wayback Machine?
faqs.a: Go to web.archive.org, find the "Save Page Now" box on the right, paste the full URL and click Save Page. The capture usually completes in under a minute and returns a permanent link containing the capture timestamp.

faqs.q: Can I archive a page that requires a login?
faqs.a: Not through a public archive, which visits as an anonymous user. Save your own PDF and full-page screenshot while you are signed in, and keep both, since these are the only copies that will exist.

faqs.q: Is a PDF good enough for long-term archiving?
faqs.a: For most purposes yes, especially if the fonts are embedded. For legal, medical or institutional records, convert to PDF/A, which is standardised as ISO 19005 and forbids external dependencies so the file renders the same decades later.

faqs.q: What is link rot?
faqs.a: The gradual disappearance of web pages that other pages link to. Pew Research Center found that 38 percent of pages online in 2013 were gone by 2023. It affects citations, news articles and government pages alike.

faqs.q: Does archiving a page break copyright?
faqs.a: Saving a personal copy for reference is generally accepted in most jurisdictions. Republishing an archived copy is a different matter. Public archives such as the Internet Archive operate under their own arrangements and honour takedown requests.
